text: Last lesson drew the boundary between what SOAR automates and what it doesn't. Now you build the real thing: a Sentinel Automation Rule paired with a Logic App playbook, wired together so a matching incident triggers a real workflow automatically, the moment it's created.

Every Automation Rule has the same three parts. A trigger — incident created or updated. A set of AND/OR conditions evaluated against the incident and its entities — severity, analytic rule name, an entity matching a value. And actions, evaluated top to bottom — run a playbook, change status, assign an owner, add a tag. A realistic condition set scopes the playbook to incidents where enrichment is actually worth the API calls, not every informational alert.

The playbook itself starts from the Microsoft Sentinel connector's incident trigger, which hands your workflow the full incident object — its ARM ID, severity, title, and extracted entities. Get_incident pulls the full record, and Add_comment_to_incident writes a visible note onto it. runAfter is how Logic Apps sequences those steps, so the comment only fires once the incident lookup has actually succeeded.

Back in Sentinel, under Automation Rules, you choose Run playbook and point it at that Logic App. The first time you do, Sentinel will prompt you to grant the Microsoft Sentinel Automation Contributor role on the playbook's resource group — skip that, and the trigger call gets rejected before your workflow ever runs.

Don't wait for a real incident to find out if it works. Trigger it manually from an existing incident and watch Logic Apps Run history, or fire a disposable test incident in a non-production workspace. Run history shows every action's raw inputs and outputs, which is where real debugging actually happens.

Next lesson takes this same playbook further: instead of just a comment, you'll pull real enrichment data — user risk, asset criticality, geo-IP — into the incident before a human ever opens it, so the first look already comes with answers instead of open questions.
